transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Good morning. What can I do for you?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: I want to report a theft. I had some things stolen out of my bag yesterday.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Right, so I'll need to take a few details. Can I start with your name?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Louise Taylor.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: OK, thank you. And are you resident in the UK?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: No. I'm actually <q id="1">Canadian</q>, though my mother was British.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: And your date of birth?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: December 14th, 1977.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: So you're just visiting this country?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: That's right. I come over most summers on business. I'm an interior designer and I come over to buy old <q id="2">furniture</q>, antiques you know. There are some really lovely things around here, but you need to get out to the small towns. I've had a really good trip this year, until this happened.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: OK. So you've been here quite a while?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Yes, I'm here for two months. I go back next week.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: So may I ask where you're staying now?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Well at present I've got a place at <q id="3">Park</q> Apartments, that's on King Street. I was staying at the Riverside Apartments on the same street, but the apartment there was only available for six weeks so I had to find another one.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: OK. And the apartment number?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Fifteen.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Now, I need to take some details of the theft. So you said you had some things stolen out of your bag?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: And were you actually carrying the bag when the theft took place?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Yes. I really can't understand it. I had my backpack on. And I went into a supermarket to buy a few things and when I opened it up my wallet wasn't there.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: And what did your wallet have in it?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Well, fortunately I don't keep my credit cards in that wallet – I keep them with my passport in an inside compartment in my backpack. But there was quite a bit of cash there ... about <q id="4">£250</q> sterling, I should think. I withdrew £300 from my account yesterday, but I did a bit of shopping, so I must have already spent about £50 of that.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: At first I thought, oh I must have left the wallet back in the apartment, but then I realised my <q id="5">phone</q> had gone as well. It was only a week old, and that's when I realised I'd been robbed. Anyway at least they didn't take the keys to my rental car.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Yes. So you say the theft occurred yesterday?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: So that was <q id="6">September the tenth.</q> And do you have any idea at all of where or when the things might possibly have been stolen?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Well at first I couldn't believe it because the bag had been on my back ever since I left the apartment after lunch. It's just a small backpack, but I generally use it when I'm travelling because it seems safer than a handbag. Anyway, I met up with a friend, and we spent a couple of hours in the <q id="7">museum.</q> But I do remember that as we were leaving there, at about 4 o'clock, a group of young boys ran up to us, and they were really crowding round us, and they were asking us what <q id="8">time</q> it was, then all of a sudden they ran off.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Can you remember anything about them?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: The one who did most of the talking was wearing a T-shirt with a picture of something ... let's see ... a tiger.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Right. Any idea of how old he might have been?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Around twelve years old?

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: And can you remember anything else about his appearance?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Not much. He was quite thin ...

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Colour of hair?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: I do remember that – he was <q id="9">blond.</q> All the others were dark-haired.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: And any details of the others?

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Not really. They came and went so quickly.

transcript.speaker: OFFICER
transcript.text: Right. So what I'm going to do now is give you a crime reference number so you can contact your insurance company. So this is ten digits: <q id="10">87954 82361.</q>

transcript.speaker: LOUISE
transcript.text: Thank you. So should I ...

Good morning everyone. My name's Janet Parker and I'm the human resources manager. We're very happy to welcome you to your new apprenticeship. I hope that the next six months will be a positive and enjoyable experience for you.

I'd like to start with some general advice about being an apprentice. Most of you have very little or no experience of working for a big organisation and the first week or so may be quite challenging. There will be a lot of new information to take in but don't worry too much about trying to remember everything. The important thing is to <q id="11">check with someone if you're not sure what to do</q> – you'll find your supervisor is very approachable and won't mind explaining things or helping you out. You're here to learn so make the most of that opportunity. You'll be spending time in different departments during your first week so make an effort to <q id="12">talk to as many people as possible</q> about their work – you'll make some new friends and find out lots of useful information.

As well as having a supervisor, you'll each be assigned a mentor. This person will be someone who's recently completed an apprenticeship and you'll meet with them on a weekly basis. Their role is to provide help and support throughout your apprenticeship. Of course, this doesn't mean they'll actually do any of your work for you – instead they'll be asking you about <q id="13">what goals you've achieved so far,</q> as well as helping you to <q id="13">identify any areas for improvement.</q> You can also <q id="14">discuss your more long-term ambitions</q> with them as well.

Now I just want to run through a few company policies for our apprenticeship scheme with you... Most importantly, the internet. As part of your job you'll be doing some research online so obviously you'll have unlimited access for that but please <q id="15">don't use it for personal use</q> – you'll have your own phones for that.

Some of you have already asked me about flexible working. After your probationary three-month period – some of you will be eligible for this – but <q id="16">it will depend on which department you're in and what your personal circumstances are.</q> So please don't assume you'll automatically be permitted to do this.

I want to make sure there's no confusion about our holiday policy. Apart from any statutory public holidays <q id="17">we ask that you don't book any holidays until after your six-month apprenticeship has finished.</q> Time off should only be taken if you are unwell. Please speak to your supervisor if this is going to be a problem.

You'll be expected to work a 40-hour week but there may be opportunities to do overtime during busy periods. Although you're not required to do this, <q id="18">it can be a valuable experience – so we advise you to take it up if possible.</q> Obviously, we understand that people do have commitments outside work, so don't worry if there are times when you are unavailable.

As you know, we don't have a formal dress code here – you may wear casual clothes as long as they're practical – and the only restriction for shoes we have is on high heels for health and safety reasons. <q id="19">Comfortable shoes like trainers are preferable.</q>

There's a heavily subsidised canteen on site where you can get hot meals or salads cheaply. Snacks and drinks are also provided – so <q id="20">we've decided to introduce a no packed lunch policy.</q> This is partly to encourage healthy eating at work and partly to stop people from eating at their workstation, which is unhygienic.
OK moving on to ...

transcript.speaker: TUTOR
transcript.text: OK, so what I'd like you to do now is to talk to your partner about your presentations on urban planning. You should have done most of the reading now, so I'd like you to share your ideas, and talk about the structure of your presentation and what you need to do next.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: OK Rob. I'm glad we chose quite a specific topic – cities built next to the sea. It made it much easier to find relevant information.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: Yeah. And cities are growing so quickly – I mean, we know that more than half the world's population lives in cities now.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Yeah, though that's all cities, not just ones on the coast. But <q id="21">most of the biggest cities are actually built by the sea,</q> I'd not realised that before.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: Nor me. And what's more, a lot of them are built at places where rivers come out into the sea. But apparently this can be a problem.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: Well, as the city expands, agriculture and industry tend to spread further inland along the rivers, and so agriculture moves even further inland up the river. That's not necessarily a problem, except <q id="22">it means more and more pollutants are discharged into the rivers.</q>

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: So these are brought downstream to the cities?

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: Right. Hmm. Did you read that article about Miami, on the east coast of the USA?

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: Well, apparently back in the 1950s they built channels to drain away the water in case of flooding.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Sounds sensible.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: Yeah, they spent quite a lot of money on them. <q id="23">But what they didn't take into account was global warming.</q> So they built the drainage channels too close to sea level, and now sea levels are rising, they're more or less useless. If there's a lot of rain, the water can't run away, there's nowhere for it to go. The whole design was faulty.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: So what are the authorities doing about it now?

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: I don't know. I did read that they're aiming to stop disposing of waste water into the ocean over the next ten years.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: But that won't help with flood prevention now, will it?

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: No. Really <q id="24">they just need to find the money for something to replace the drainage channels,</q> in order to protect against flooding now. But in the long term they need to consider the whole ecosystem.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Right. Really, though, coastal cities can't deal with their problems on their own, can they? I mean, they've got to start acting together at an international level instead of just doing their own thing.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: Absolutely. The thing is, everyone knows what the problems are and environmentalists have a pretty good idea of what we should be doing about them, so <q id="25">they should be able to work together</q> to some extent. But it's going to be a long time before countries come to a decision on what principles they're prepared to abide by.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Yes, if they ever do.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: So I think we've probably got enough for our presentation. It's only fifteen minutes.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: OK. So I suppose we'll begin with some general historical background about why coastal cities were established. But <q id="26">we don't want to spend too long on that,</q> the other students will already know a bit about it. It's all to do with communications and so on.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Yes. We should mention some geographical factors, things like wetlands and river estuaries and coastal erosion and so on. We could have some maps of different cities with these features marked.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: On a handout you mean? Or <q id="27">some slides everyone can see?</q>

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Yeah, that'd be better.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: It'd be good to go into past mistakes in a bit more detail. Did you read that case study of the problems there were in New Orleans with flooding a few years ago?

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Yes. <q id="28">We could use that as the basis for that part of the talk.</q> I don't think the other students will have read it, but they'll remember hearing about the flooding at the time.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: OK. So that's probably enough background.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: So then we'll go on to talk about what action's being taken to deal with the problems of coastal cities.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: OK. What else do we need to talk about? Maybe something on future risks, looking more at the long term, if populations continue to grow.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: Yeah. We'll need to do a bit of work there, I haven't got much information, have you?

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: No. <q id="29">We'll need to look at some websites.</q> Shouldn't take too long.

transcript.speaker: CARLA
transcript.text: OK. And I think we should end by talking about international implications. Maybe <q id="30">we could ask people in the audience.</q> We've got people from quite a lot of different places.

transcript.speaker: ROB
transcript.text: That'd be interesting, if we have time, yes. So now shall we ...

Producing enough energy to meet our needs has become a serious problem. Demand is rising rapidly, because of the world's increasing population and expanding <q id="31">industry.</q> Burning fossil fuels, like gas, coal and oil, seriously damages the environment and they'll eventually run out. For a number of years now, scientists have been working out how we can derive energy from renewable sources, such as the sun and wind, without causing pollution. Today I'll outline marine renewable energy – also called ocean energy – which harnesses the movement of the oceans.
Marine renewable energy can be divided into three main categories: wave energy, tidal energy and ocean thermal energy conversion, and I'll say a few words about each one.

First, wave energy. Numerous devices have been invented to harvest wave energy, with names such as Wave Dragon, the Penguin and Mighty Whale, and research is going on to try and come up with a really efficient method. This form of energy has plenty of potential, as the source is <q id="32">constant,</q> and there's no danger of waves coming to a standstill. Electricity can be generated using onshore systems, using a reservoir, or offshore systems. But the problem with ocean waves is that they're erratic, with the wind making them travel in every <q id="33">direction.</q> This adds to the difficulty of creating efficient technology: ideally all the waves would travel smoothly and regularly along the same straight line. Another drawback is that sand and other sediment on the ocean <q id="34">floor</q> might be stopped from flowing normally, which can lead to environmental problems.

The second category of marine energy that I'll mention is tidal energy. One major advantage of using the tide, rather than waves, as a source of energy is that it's <q id="35">predictable:</q> we know the exact times of high and low tides for years to come.

For tidal energy to be effective, the difference between high and low tides needs to be at least five metres, and this occurs naturally in only about forty places on Earth. But the right conditions can be created by constructing a tidal lagoon, an area of sea water separated from the sea.

One current plan is to create a tidal lagoon on the coast of Wales. This will be an area of water within a <q id="36">bay</q> at Swansea, sheltered by a U-shaped breakwater, or dam, built out from the coast. The breakwater will contain sixteen hydro turbines, and as the tide rises, water rushes through the breakwater, activating the turbines, which turn a generator to produce electricity. Then, for three hours as the tide goes out, the water is held back within the breakwater, increasing the difference in water level, until it's several metres higher within the lagoon than in the open sea. Then, in order to release the stored water, <q id="37">gates</q> in the breakwater are opened. It pours powerfully out of the lagoon, driving the turbines in the breakwater in the opposite direction and again generating thousands of megawatts of electricity. As there are two high tides a day, this lagoon scheme would generate electricity four times a day, every day, for a total of around 14 hours in every 24 – and enough electricity for over 150,000 homes.

This system has quite a lot in its favour: unlike solar and wind energy it doesn't depend on the weather; the turbines are operated without the need for <q id="38">fuel,</q> so it doesn't create any greenhouse gas emissions; and very little maintenance is needed. It's estimated that electricity generated in this way will be relatively cheap, and that manufacturing the components would create more than 2,000 <q id="39">jobs,</q> a big boost to the local economy.

On the other hand, there are fears that lagoons might harm both fish and birds, for example by disturbing <q id="40">migration</q> patterns, and causing a build-up of silt, affecting local ecosystems.

There are other forms of tidal energy, but I'll go on to the third category of marine energy: ocean thermal energy conversion. This depends on there being a big difference in temperature between surface water and the water a couple of kilometres below the surface, and this occurs in tropical coastal areas.
